title: Brand impersonation through deceptive domains
content: A brand name in a hostname, subdomain, or URL path does not prove ownership. Compare the registrable domain with a trusted allowlist and treat an unrelated registrable domain as impersonation evidence.

title: Registered-domain verification
content: The registrable domain is the authoritative ownership boundary for ordinary URL analysis. A subdomain such as accounts.example.com is controlled by example.com, while google.com.evil.com is controlled by evil.com.

title: Typosquatting
content: Typosquatting uses insertion, deletion, substitution, transposition, or lookalike characters to resemble a protected brand. Strong similarity to an official brand is malicious identity evidence even when an ML model is benign.

title: Character substitution
content: Replacing letters with digits or visually similar characters, such as g00gle for google, is a common typosquatting technique and should be recorded as character-substitution evidence.

title: Unicode homographs
content: Unicode characters that resemble ASCII letters can create homograph attacks. Mixed scripts and confusable characters should be treated as deception indicators.

title: Punycode domains
content: An xn-- label represents an internationalized domain name. Punycode is not automatically malicious, but unexpected or brand-confusable Punycode requires additional scrutiny.

title: Mixed-script domains
content: A hostname combining scripts such as Latin and Cyrillic can hide lookalike characters. Mixed-script evidence is stronger when it targets a known brand.

title: Threat intelligence interpretation
content: A confirmed match in a verified phishing or malware feed is strong evidence. Feed status and source metadata should be preserved for auditability.

title: ML false positives
content: ML probability is supporting evidence, not definitive proof. Legitimate login pages and complex URLs can produce high phishing probabilities, so verified identity can downgrade an ML suspicion.

title: ML false negatives
content: A low ML probability does not clear a URL when stronger identity evidence detects typosquatting, brand mismatch, or homograph deception.

title: Official-domain verification
content: An official domain match can support a safe decision when no confirmed critical threat evidence contradicts it. Legitimate subdomains inherit ownership from their registrable domain.

title: HTTPS and TLS interpretation
content: HTTPS encrypts transport but does not prove that a website is legitimate. Attackers can obtain certificates for deceptive domains, so HTTPS must not override identity or threat evidence.

title: Suspicious subdomains
content: A brand in a subdomain is not proof of ownership. In google.com.evil.com, the registrable domain is evil.com; the Google label is deceptive context.

title: Deceptive URL paths
content: A brand name in a path can be used to imitate a login or payment page. Path text is supporting context and cannot establish domain ownership.

title: Malware versus phishing
content: Phishing primarily seeks credentials or sensitive information, while malware delivery seeks execution or compromise. A URL can have evidence for either or both categories.

title: Unknown threat intelligence state
content: Absence from a threat feed does NOT mean safe. Unknown means the queried source has no confirmed record or cannot establish a verdict.

title: Newly created malicious domains
content: New malicious domains may not yet appear in feeds. Lack of historical evidence should not suppress strong identity, lexical, DNS, or behavioral indicators.

title: Domain reputation
content: Domain reputation is contextual evidence. A domain with poor reputation can support suspicion, but reputation alone should not replace verified intelligence or ownership analysis.

title: DNS anomalies
content: Rapidly changing records, suspicious hosting, or unusual DNS configuration can support investigation. DNS anomalies are supporting evidence and require corroboration.

title: Evidence contradiction arbitration
content: When ML says suspicious but official identity is verified, record ML_HIGH_SUSPICION plus OFFICIAL_IDENTITY and mark ML_DOWNGRADED. When ML says legitimate but impersonation evidence is strong, record ML_IMPERSONATION_CONFLICT and let stronger identity evidence prevail.
